sections.heading: Key points
sections.content:
*   Romantic love inherited many of the expectations once placed upon religion.
*   Asking one person to provide everything makes disappointment inevitable.
*   Love enlarges one's world; dependency asks another person to fill it.

![Image 15: To grow, the lobster must first shed its shell.](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/styles/article_inline_half_caption/public/field_blog_entry_images/2026-09/still_life_with_a_lobster.jpg?itok=qFgBvFNX)

To grow, the lobster must first shed its shell.

Source: Wikimedia Commons/Jan de Heem/Public domain

When worldly ambition fails to validate us, we often turn to [romantic love](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/relationships "Psychology Today looks at romantic love"). We rely on another person to lend our life weight and meaning. First, we ask the crowd; then, we ask one person.

The Greeks had several words for love: _eros_, _philia_, _storge_, and _agape_. Eros is passionate love, philia is [friendship](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/friends "Psychology Today looks at friendship"), storge is familial love, and agape is universal love. But we reduce all these types of love into just one word, which we associate with romantic love.

sections.heading: The Rise of Romantic Love
sections.content:
What we don’t realise is that romantic love, unlike passionate love, is a fairly modern concept. If you think about it, romantic love barely features in the 73 books of the Bible. The Bible’s greatest love stories are David and Jonathan, Ruth and Naomi, and, above all, the love of man for God. In the ancient world, passionate love was not seen as ennobling but as a dangerous affliction: think only of Helen and Paris, Dido and Aeneas, Antony and Cleopatra.

How, then, did this dangerous affliction become our highest ideal? As religion retreated, our need for religion remained. We still longed for meaning and transcendence. Gradually, the sacred seeped out of God and into romantic love. We stopped loving God and began loving love.

That’s why love speaks the language of religion: adoration, devotion, eternal union. We expect one person to provide us with everything: intimacy, friendship, intellectual stimulation—until death do us part.

sections.heading: What Love Really Is
sections.content:
But once a person is given the role of God, disappointment becomes inevitable. When things go wrong, we conclude that we chose the wrong person, or that love has died—not that we are asking far too much.

This brings us back to the original question: What is love? Beneath all its forms—philia, eros, storge, agape—love is a reaching out beyond ourselves towards someone or something that lends weight and meaning to our life. It is the force that enables us to cross the [boundary](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/boundaries "Psychology Today looks at boundary") between ourselves and the world—to shed our shell, like a lobster, and grow beyond it. That’s why people of little love are so small.

This definition of love is useful, in that it gives us a litmus test by which to distinguish love from mere dependency. We can ask: Is this person enlarging my world, or am I merely asking them to save me from myself? Are we growing together, or merely leaning against one another?

**You may also be interested in my companion piece,**[**Can Romantic Love Save Us?**](https://neelburton.com/2026/06/28/how-romantic-love-became-our-new-religion/)

# What Is Love?

## How to distinguish true love from mere dependency.

### Key points

*   Romantic love inherited many of the expectations once placed upon religion.
*   Asking one person to provide everything makes disappointment inevitable.
*   Love enlarges one's world; dependency asks another person to fill it.

![Image 15: To grow, the lobster must first shed its shell.](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/styles/article_inline_half_caption/public/field_blog_entry_images/2026-09/still_life_with_a_lobster.jpg?itok=qFgBvFNX)

To grow, the lobster must first shed its shell.

Source: Wikimedia Commons/Jan de Heem/Public domain

When worldly ambition fails to validate us, we often turn to [romantic love](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/relationships "Psychology Today looks at romantic love"). We rely on another person to lend our life weight and meaning. First, we ask the crowd; then, we ask one person.

The Greeks had several words for love: _eros_, _philia_, _storge_, and _agape_. Eros is passionate love, philia is [friendship](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/friends "Psychology Today looks at friendship"), storge is familial love, and agape is universal love. But we reduce all these types of love into just one word, which we associate with romantic love.

## The Rise of Romantic Love

What we don’t realise is that romantic love, unlike passionate love, is a fairly modern concept. If you think about it, romantic love barely features in the 73 books of the Bible. The Bible’s greatest love stories are David and Jonathan, Ruth and Naomi, and, above all, the love of man for God. In the ancient world, passionate love was not seen as ennobling but as a dangerous affliction: think only of Helen and Paris, Dido and Aeneas, Antony and Cleopatra.

How, then, did this dangerous affliction become our highest ideal? As religion retreated, our need for religion remained. We still longed for meaning and transcendence. Gradually, the sacred seeped out of God and into romantic love. We stopped loving God and began loving love.

That’s why love speaks the language of religion: adoration, devotion, eternal union. We expect one person to provide us with everything: intimacy, friendship, intellectual stimulation—until death do us part.

## What Love Really Is

But once a person is given the role of God, disappointment becomes inevitable. When things go wrong, we conclude that we chose the wrong person, or that love has died—not that we are asking far too much.

This brings us back to the original question: What is love? Beneath all its forms—philia, eros, storge, agape—love is a reaching out beyond ourselves towards someone or something that lends weight and meaning to our life. It is the force that enables us to cross the [boundary](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/boundaries "Psychology Today looks at boundary") between ourselves and the world—to shed our shell, like a lobster, and grow beyond it. That’s why people of little love are so small.

This definition of love is useful, in that it gives us a litmus test by which to distinguish love from mere dependency. We can ask: Is this person enlarging my world, or am I merely asking them to save me from myself? Are we growing together, or merely leaning against one another?
